heading: Start with the kind of birding you enjoy
intro: You do not need a long species list to enjoy an outing. Tell the provider whether you are learning to use binoculars, hoping to photograph a few birds or pursuing detailed identifications. Those interests can call for different explanations and pacing. A shared nature excursion may suit a beginner; a more focused request needs a specific discussion about the guide and proposed program.
points: Describe your experience level and the interests of everyone travelling.
Ask how the outing balances beginners and experienced observers.
Discuss the pace before booking a specialist program.

heading: Choose a setting, not a promised checklist
intro: The INABIO-supported Yasuní field guide documents birds in a particular biosphere-reserve study area. A regional record does not mean every lodge or trail offers the same observations. Ask which habitats your proposed outing visits and request a local checklist with its date and scope. Compare the actual base and routes instead of treating an entire destination as one observation point.
points: Ask where the list’s observations were recorded.
Clarify which routes and habitats are included in your program.
Keep target species separate from guaranteed outcomes.

heading: Learn how an identification is made
intro: A useful guide explains what supports an identification and what remains uncertain. Ask about experience with the proposed region, spoken languages and the way beginners are included. If sound identification matters to you, make that interest explicit. Leave room for a bird heard but not seen, or a brief view that cannot be named confidently, rather than insist on filling every line of a checklist.
points: Ask about the guide’s experience with local birds and calls.
Request clear distinctions between seen, heard and uncertain records.
Discuss how you will review observations after an outing.

heading: Keep equipment simple and confirmed
intro: Ask whether binoculars or a scope are provided and whether you can practise using them before leaving the base. If you bring your own camera, explain the equipment and ask how it fits the route and group pace. Storage, rain protection and carrying assistance need confirmation for the actual booking. Equipment should support a comfortable outing rather than dictate every stop.
points: Confirm which observation equipment is included and shared.
Ask about walking, standing, boarding and resting opportunities.
Plan how to carry your own equipment on the agreed route.

heading: Observe without staging the scene
intro: Choose an observation approach that gives birds space and respects the guide’s instructions. Do not approach a nest, chase a bird or move vegetation to improve a photograph. Ask about the provider’s policy on feeding, recorded-call playback and other methods used to attract birds. A quiet look at ordinary behaviour can be more meaningful than a photograph obtained by disturbing the scene.
points: Ask how the provider avoids disturbance during observation.
Let the guide choose where the group stops and when it moves on.
Put wildlife behaviour ahead of a closer camera position.

heading: Build an itinerary with room to observe
intro: Ask for the full program, including the base, transfers and the time available for observation. A short package name does not explain how much of each day is spent travelling. Confirm what happens if weather or route conditions change an outing and review current regional advice for the gateways. Select a plan you understand, with space for the interests and physical needs of your group.
points: Request the proposed outings and transfer responsibilities in writing.
Clarify what can change and how alternatives are agreed.
Keep arrival and onward connections within the planning conversation.
